lesson.title: One Number for the Whole Circuit: Complex Impedance
lesson.summary: Complex impedance combines resistance and reactance into a single complex number, letting Ohm's law work directly with phasors in AC circuits.
lesson.body:
Resistance alone cannot describe how an AC circuit containing inductors or capacitors responds to a sinusoidal source, because those elements shift the phase of current relative to voltage as well as scaling its magnitude. Complex impedance, Z, solves this by packaging both effects, magnitude scaling and phase shifting, into a single complex number: Z = R + jX, where R is resistance and X is net reactance, XL − XC. Impedance is measured in ohms, and it plays exactly the role resistance plays in Ohm's law, except that voltage and current are now phasors and Z is complex.

In polar form, Z = |Z|∠θ, where |Z| = √(R² + X²) is the impedance magnitude and θ = arctan(X/R) is the impedance angle. This angle is not arbitrary: it is exactly the phase angle by which current lags, or leads, voltage in that branch, which is why impedance connects so directly to the phasor diagrams already introduced. A purely resistive circuit has θ = 0°, current in phase with voltage; a purely inductive circuit has θ = 90°, current lagging by a full quarter cycle; a purely capacitive circuit has θ = −90°, current leading.

Take the running series RL circuit with R = 30 Ω and XL = 40 Ω. The impedance is Z = 30 + j40 Ω. Its magnitude is |Z| = √(30² + 40²) = √(900 + 1600) = √2500 = 50 Ω, and its angle is θ = arctan(40/30) = arctan(1.333) = 53.13°, so Z = 50∠53.13° Ω. Applying this branch across the source V = 120∠0° V rms and using the phasor form of Ohm's law, I = V/Z: I = 120∠0° / 50∠53.13° = (120/50)∠(0° − 53.13°) = 2.4∠−53.13° A, exactly the current phasor used in the phasor diagram and phasor addition worked examples.

Dividing complex numbers in polar form is simple, divide the magnitudes and subtract the angles, which is precisely why phasors and polar form pay off together: Ohm's law, V = IZ, becomes a one-line calculation instead of a differential equation. Series impedances add just like series resistances, Z_total = Z1 + Z2 + ..., because Kirchhoff's voltage law in phasor form, established in the phasor addition section, guarantees it; parallel impedances combine with the same reciprocal rule as parallel resistors. Impedance is therefore the single quantity that unlocks every steady-state AC circuit technique already familiar from DC circuits, mesh analysis, nodal analysis, Thevenin equivalents, once resistances are simply replaced by complex impedances.

Impedance is also frequency dependent, since reactance itself depends on ω, so the very same physical circuit presents a different impedance, and therefore a different current magnitude and phase shift, at different frequencies. A series RL circuit that looks almost purely resistive at 60 Hz can look almost purely inductive at 6000 Hz, because XL = ωL grows linearly with frequency while R stays fixed. This frequency dependence is exactly what makes RLC circuits useful as filters, passing some frequencies while blocking others, a behavior impedance makes possible to calculate precisely.
